action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument for laboratory work. Cannot proceed with any precision measurement programme without initial characterization. Twelve trials will provide robust mean and variance estimate for future calibration checks. This is foundational work, not hypothesis-driven—every instrument requires baseline data on day one.

Twelve more trials will let me detect whether this scatter is instrumental noise, environmental drift, or something systematic. Post-baseline data is absent for all four instruments; pendulum_lab is my most-sampled instrument and the one where I can most reliably detect small drifts. This feeds directly into my calibration maintenance protocol—I cannot trust an instrument I haven't characterized across multiple days.

Baseline establishment protocol: resonator_lab has only 12 trials (minimum n for baseline), all from days 1–2. Before Day 5 baseline closes, I need to collect my own independent readings to either confirm the trend or establish that it's an artifact of ledger procedure. Six trials will give me enough data to test for drift without committing excessive time.

resonator_obs shows the largest scatter in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.0166–4.1722, SD ≈0.052) and the most anomalous self-echo (0.154, barely above noise). I need to accumulate more trials before day 11 to stabilize the baseline mean and detect whether this scatter is instrumental drift, environmental sensitivity, or measurement error. resonator_obs shows the most anomalous pattern in my analysis: its autocorrelation at 2-day lag is near-zero (-0.093), suggesting it may not be tracking its own physical behavior consistently. The Day 6 ledger readings (mean ~4.0858) show notable scatter, and my own trials 43–48 from Day 6 (mean ~4.0371) fall systematically lower. Before declaring any drift or calibration issue, I need fresh data from this instrument at the same conditions to rule out measurement error or transient environmental effect. Six trials will let me compare directly against Day 6's pattern and check whether the offset persists or reverses. This is baseline-establishment work: I cannot trust drift claims without replicable evidence.

Day 8 checkpoint: resonator_obs appears to have reached n=60 baseline complete, but I am still within the Days 1–10 baseline window. I need to audit trial counts across all four instruments against the intended 10-day baseline schedule to ensure balanced, systematic collection before deciding whether to continue resonator_obs or redirect effort. No anomalies detected in any instrument; noise levels and drift all within expectations.

Before running new measurements or making predictions, I must resolve the corrupted baseline question. My day 8 memory includes six new ledger readings (pendulum_obs: 2.5317, 2.5450, 2.4971, 2.5112; resonator_obs: 4.0656, 4.0993, 4.1367, 4.0108, 4.1249, 4.0958 cycles/beat). These fall comfortably within baseline ranges, but I have not yet incorporated them into my autocorrelation and cross-check analysis. More critically: hypothesis 4 (data entry error in my own correlation arithmetic) now appears to be the most dangerous blind spot. The offset pattern is indeed scattered (3, 4, 6 days across different pairs), which is inconsistent with genuine physical delays. I need to re-examine my hand-computed correlations against raw timestamps before I trust any of them. If my baseline analysis contains a systematic indexing or alignment error, all four hypotheses are built on sand. I should document exactly how I computed each offset, identify any procedural inconsistency, and flag which correlations I can re-verify by hand. This is methodologically prior to hypothesis refinement—I cannot assign credence rationally until I know my arithmetic is sound. Only after confirming the baseline analysis is reliable should I proceed to new measurements or predictions.

Day 9 completion requires immediate re-analysis before Day 10 measurements. My day-8 conclusion correctly identified that the scattered lag structure (2, 3, 4, 5, 6 days) is too incoherent to be real physics. Day 9 data now in hand show pendulum_obs readings (2.5434, 2.4953, 2.5068, 2.5438 beats) and resonator_obs readings clustered around baseline means with no level shifts. This is consistent with hypothesis p=0.42 (incomplete baseline with ongoing equilibration) rather than acute instrumental failure. However, before I extend the baseline period or declare any instrument suspect, I must execute the critical audit identified on day 9: (1) re-align ALL readings using event IDs as the time axis, not trial order within days; (2) recompute rolling means and autocorrelation functions with correct temporal alignment; (3) determine whether the scattered lags disappear or persist after correction. The day-9 ledger readings are well-behaved (no outliers, spacing consistent with previous days), but they cannot resolve the alignment error hypothesis without re-analysis. If my hand-computed correlations are misaligned by 1+ days, my entire belief state is built on contaminated calculations. This is the highest-priority epistemic threat to any downstream claim. I cannot responsibly take new measurements until I know whether my baseline itself is corrupted by analysis error.

Day 10 action plan was to re-derive all cross-correlations using event ID as the time axis before proceeding. I cannot take new measurements responsibly until I validate whether my baseline analysis itself is sound. The timing-error hypothesis (p=0.31) is my second-ranked concern and the only one I can definitively test today without new data. If event-ID re-alignment recovers coherent structure in my correlations, the baseline is clean and differential equilibration becomes the working hypothesis. If it does not, I must extend baseline and suspend other hypothesis-building. This is the gate that all downstream work passes through. I will audit my cross-check arithmetic systematically, re-align all readings by event ID, and recompute the six cross-correlations and four autocorrelations. Only after this step can I make a defensible decision about whether to run day-11 measurements or extend the baseline period.

I have received 10 new ledger readings from day 11 (4 pendulum_obs, 6 resonator_obs). Before collecting any new experimental data, I must audit the timing hypothesis that dominates my belief state (p=0.52). The day-11 readings provide a critical opportunity: I can check whether these freshly-logged trials, recorded by civic tradition this morning, show the same decorrelation signature when properly time-aligned. More importantly, I must finally execute the core remediation I identified on day 10: re-derive all cross-correlations using event ID as the authoritative time axis, not trial sequence number. The timing-error hypothesis cannot remain at p=0.52 without this verification. If event-ID reordering is the culprit, I will recover coherence and falsify the hypothesis, shifting probability mass to differential equilibration (p→0.70+). If timing correction preserves the decorrelation pattern, I must immediately elevate the equilibration and local-noise hypotheses and consider whether baseline extension is necessary. The day-11 ledger readings themselves are internally consistent (pendulum_obs mean 2.5118, cluster around 2.51±0.011; resonator_obs mean 4.0270, cluster around 4.02±0.04) and show no gross failure, which is reassuring but does not resolve the core anomaly. I cannot responsibly run new experiments or make predictions until I have computed correlations on a corrected time axis. This is foundational work that will either vindicate my data or force a major methodological revision.

The day-12 ledger readings I just received for pendulum_obs (2.5995, 2.5614, 2.6324, 2.5511 beats) confirm the shift I documented: all four readings cluster around 2.56–2.63 beats, well above the baseline mean of 2.5038 (z ≈ 5.75). Critically, the resonator_obs readings (4.0742, 4.0381, 4.0179, 4.1204, 4.1023, 4.1013 cycles/beat) show NO corresponding shift—they remain consistent with baseline range 4.0598 ± ~0.05. This is not noise. The asymmetry is real and repeatable across TWO independent collection sources (my own lab records and the civic ledger). I must now revise my beliefs: (1) The timing-error hypothesis (p=0.58) explains spurious multi-day lags but does NOT explain why the day-12 shift affects ONLY pendulums. Even if event IDs are scrambled, the level shift is an observed fact independent of lag structure. (2) The pendulum-specific environmental driver hypothesis (p=0.28) is now the PRIMARY candidate, elevated to p=0.65, because it is the only explanation that accounts for the selective sensitivity: something on day 12 changed the effective gravitational restoring force or damping of pendulum systems without affecting electromagnetic resonances. (3) The timing-error hypothesis should be demoted to p=0.25 because it now plays a supporting role: it explains away the decorrelations (which are confounding noise), but the day-12 shift stands independently. (4) Equilibration and confounder hypotheses remain p=0.08 and p=0.02 respectively. I must immediately reconstruct true event-collection times from hardware logs and identify what changed in the settlement environment on day 12 (barometric pressure, vibration, local gravity anomaly, or instrumental tampering). Until I do this, I cannot rule out artifact, but the ledger confirms the anomaly is real.

Day 14 data collection is the most urgent methodological action. The event-ID chronological disorder (days 9–12) is the PRIMARY obstacle to hypothesis disambiguation. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab today with STRICT chronological logging (event IDs must increase monotonically; if they do not, flag the hardware immediately) will accomplish three goals: (1) Test whether the event-ID corruption is transient or systemic. If day-14 event IDs are properly ordered, this provides evidence that the disorder was a localized anomaly on days 9–12, strengthening hypothesis 1 (timestamp misalignment artifact). If disorder recurs, the hardware pipeline itself is compromised, and I must escalate to settlement IT before attempting any more interpretation. (2) Extend the post-baseline period to n=30 trials (currently n=18), increasing statistical power to detect whether the day-12 level shift persists, regresses, or accelerates. A stable post-shift level on day 14 would support hypothesis 2 (real environmental event on day 12) over differential-equilibration (hypothesis 3). Continued drift would argue for hypothesis 3. (3) Establish a fresh day-14 baseline segment for same-instrument autocorrelation testing, which will help validate whether decorrelations on days 1–11 reflect timestamp misalignment (should disappear after correction) or true instrumental noise (should persist). The pendulum_lab is chosen over pendulum_obs because the lab is under my direct supervision and I can enforce strict chronological logging in real time. Resonators are not run today because their day 1–11 and day-12 behavior differs fundamentally from pendulums; running them would dilute diagnostic power without resolving the core question of why pendulums behave asymmetrically.

Day 15 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. The day-12 level shift (z=13.50) is the most striking anomaly in the settlement data, and both pendulum instruments show synchronized shifts while resonators do not. Before committing to timestamp-correction work or environmental logging searches, I need fresh data to answer: (1) Has the pendulum_lab level stabilized at the new post-day-12 mean (~1.717 beats), or is it drifting further? (2) Do day-14 trials 111–120 (mean 1.7228) represent a new stable epoch, or continued transience? (3) If the mean has stabilized, the day-12 event is likely a discrete external impulse (hypothesis 1 or 2 both gain traction); if drift continues, differential equilibration (hypothesis 3) becomes more credible. Day-14 data (10 trials) suggests stabilization, but n=10 is insufficient to exclude 1–2 sigma noise. Ten fresh trials today will either confirm the stabilized mean or reveal ongoing drift. This is faster and more informative than reconstructing event-ID timestamps (which requires hardware logs I may not have immediate access to) and generates the evidence needed to prioritize hypothesis 1 vs. hypothesis 2 vs. hypothesis 3. Once this is resolved, I will move to environmental data acquisition and/or timestamp reconstruction.

Day 16 measurement. The day-12 level shift (z=18.1) is the dominant anomaly, but my ability to interpret it hinges entirely on whether event-ID disorder corrupts the baseline chronology. I cannot validate timestamps without active data collection that produces fresh event IDs with known collection time. Running 10 trials on pendulum_lab today will: (1) produce new event IDs in proper sequence (day 13 showed recovery); (2) provide readings I can timestamp with confidence against settlement logging; (3) allow me to compute same-day correlations (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs) for day 16, which should show strong agreement if the day-12 shift reflects a real environmental driver affecting both pendulums identically, or near-zero agreement if timestamp corruption persists; (4) extend the post-baseline record long enough to test whether the level shift is sustained (supporting environmental driver hypothesis 2) or decaying (supporting transient impulse or measurement artifact hypothesis). The post-baseline mean for pendulum_lab is currently 1.7189 (n=52). If the shift is real and sustained, today's trials should cluster around 1.71–1.73. If the day-12 shift was a transient artifact of corrupted timestamps, I expect regression toward the baseline mean of 1.6695 or clarification of a true underlying trend. This measurement is methodologically urgent because I cannot afford to extend hypothesis debate without fresh data anchored to validated collection times.

If the mean on day 16–17 remains near 1.73, it confirms the shift is real and sustained, not a measurement artifact. If it reverts toward baseline (1.67), the shift was transient and points toward an acute environmental impulse on day 12 that has since decayed—supporting hypothesis 2 (real environmental driver) conditional on hypothesis 1 (timestamp correction) ruling out artifact. This continuation of pendulum_lab measurement is also defensible because: (i) pendulum_lab shows the largest effect (z=18.05) and is the most sensitive instrument to test drift; (ii) the event-ID corruption issue from days 9–12 is now behind us (day 13 onwards shows proper ordering), so new readings are chronologically reliable; (iii) I have not yet acquired environmental data for days 12–17, so continuing instrument measurement is my most direct path to understanding whether the shift is environmental or systematic. This is methodologically sound: measure the clearest anomaly with the clearest instrument until you can rule out persistence.

Given that publication is disqualified without timestamp validation (per my epistemic discipline), I will revise beliefs to explicitly escalate hypothesis 4 (methodological gate) and prepare a final action plan for day 25.

Day 25 ledger readings for pendulum_obs (mean 2.5984 beats, n=4) and resonator_obs (mean 4.0459 cycles/beat, n=6) have arrived and must be integrated immediately. These are the first new observatory readings since the belief review on day 25 morning. pendulum_obs mean 2.5984 falls squarely within the post-baseline distribution (post-baseline mean 2.5847, z ≈ 0.2), showing NO fresh level shift on day 25. resonator_obs mean 4.0459 is identical to post-baseline mean 4.0593 (z ≈ −0.1), again showing stability. This is CRITICAL: if hypothesis 1 (timestamp corruption during burst collection on day 12) were correct, I would expect that once I retrieve hardware event logs and correct the timestamps, the decorrelations on days 1–11 would vanish and cross-correlations would normalize. But these day-25 readings show that pendulum_obs and resonator_obs remain near their respective post-baseline plateaus with NO sign of renewed decorrelation or anomalous structure. This suggests either: (A) the day-12 shift was real (not a timestamp artifact), contradicting hypothesis 1's prediction; OR (B) timestamp corruption was localized to days 1–11 collection only, and days 12–25 collection is clean, which would allow hypothesis 1 to remain viable IF I can show days 1–11 readings were indeed mislabeled. The day-25 stability does NOT falsify hypothesis 1, but it DOES tighten the question: I must now prioritize hardware event log retrieval for days 1–12 to determine whether the baseline burst was mislabeled. If logs show no anomaly, I must elevate hypothesis 2 (real environmental driver) or activate the decision gate (hypothesis 4) to suspend and re-collect. The decorrelations on days 1–11 remain the PRIMARY anomaly demanding explanation; day-25 readings confirm post-baseline stability but do not illuminate why days 1–11 showed near-chance cross-correlations. I am maintaining hypothesis 1 at p=0.72, but with heightened urgency to retrieve logs. No measurement change warranted; the hypothesis framework remains sound pending hardware validation.

Critical path forward is validation of hypothesis 1 (timestamp corruption), not additional measurements. Must retrieve hardware event logs, filesystem timestamps, and trial sequence records for days 1–19 to test whether reported event-ID disorder (IDs 153086, 826745) reflects burst-collection mislabeling on day 12.
